title: Non-defining clauses: prepositions and quantifiers
summary: Extend non-defining relative clauses with formal preposition-plus-pronoun phrases, quantifiers such as all of whom and some of which, and which referring to a complete preceding idea rather than one noun.
learningObjectives: Choose whom for a person and which for a thing when a preposition comes immediately before a relative pronoun.
Contrast formal preposition-fronting with natural spoken clauses that place the preposition later.
Describe parts of known groups using all, some, most, none or numbers plus of whom/which.
Use a comma followed by which to comment on a whole earlier event or fact, not only one noun.

explanation.heading: Move a preposition before whom or which in formal style
explanation.body: A non-defining clause can begin with a preposition followed by whom for a person or which for a thing. This fronted arrangement is especially common in formal writing. The preposition needs to match the meaning of the earlier verb or phrase; for example, write to someone or depend on something.
explanation.example: Ms Rao, to whom I sent the documents, will reply soon.

explanation.heading: Use a more natural preposition position when speaking
explanation.body: In everyday speech, the preposition often stays after its verb: the colleague who I worked with. When the preposition is at the end, spoken English typically uses who rather than whom for a person, or sometimes omits the object relative word in defining clauses. In a non-defining clause, however, the relative word remains.
explanation.example: My former tutor, who I learnt a great deal from, moved abroad.

explanation.heading: Link a group of people with of whom
explanation.body: After mentioning an identified group of people, add information about some or all its members with all of whom, many of whom, none of whom or a number of whom. Whom follows of because the reference is to people. Match the verb to the subject of the new clause and make the amount meaningful.
explanation.example: We interviewed four volunteers, two of whom had previous experience.

explanation.heading: Link objects or quantities with of which
explanation.body: Use some of which, most of which, none of which or a number of which for things. Formal noun phrases such as the name of which are possible when referring to a thing already introduced. This adds information about part of a known set, rather than identifying the set from scratch.
explanation.example: I collected six photographs, three of which were taken at night.

explanation.heading: Use which to comment on a complete preceding fact
explanation.body: Sometimes which does not describe just one noun. After a comma, it can refer to the entire event or situation in the preceding clause. This is useful for a reaction, consequence or unexpected result. Use which here, never what or that, when linking the comment directly to that fact.
explanation.example: The meeting finished early, which gave us time for lunch.

comparisons.title: Fronted preposition and natural spoken order

left.label: Formal fronting
left.example: Aisha, with whom I worked, now lives abroad.
left.note: With comes directly before whom; this sounds formal.

right.label: Conversational order
right.example: Aisha, who I worked with, now lives abroad.
right.note: With stays after worked and who remains because the clause adds extra information.

comparisons.title: People within a group and things within a set

left.label: People: of whom
left.example: Five teachers attended, three of whom spoke Spanish.
left.note: Whom refers back to an identified group of people.

right.label: Things: of which
right.example: Five files arrived, three of which were incomplete.
right.note: Which refers back to an identified set of things.

examples.sentence: The editor, for whom I prepared the summary, has approved it.
examples.note: For whom places the preposition directly before its formal person-object pronoun.

examples.sentence: My new colleague, who I share an office with, starts on Monday.
examples.note: Conversational preposition placement is at the end of the relative clause.

examples.sentence: The seven finalists, all of whom received certificates, posed for a photograph.
examples.note: All of whom refers to every person in the previously identified group.

examples.sentence: We ordered eight cushions, two of which arrived in the wrong colour.
examples.note: Two of which selects two objects from an already mentioned set.

examples.sentence: The bus broke down, which meant we arrived late.
examples.note: Which refers to the entire fact of the breakdown, not just to the bus.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Nadia, to who I emailed the details, has replied.
commonMistakes.correct: Nadia, to whom I emailed the details, has replied.
commonMistakes.why: A fronted preposition referring to a person takes formal whom.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We tested five lamps, two of whom were faulty.
commonMistakes.correct: We tested five lamps, two of which were faulty.
commonMistakes.why: Lamps are things, so use of which rather than of whom.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The concert was postponed, what disappointed everyone.
commonMistakes.correct: The concert was postponed, which disappointed everyone.
commonMistakes.why: Which, not what, can refer back to the whole previous fact in a non-defining clause.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I met three visitors, one of which was a doctor.
commonMistakes.correct: I met three visitors, one of whom was a doctor.
commonMistakes.why: The group consists of people, so the quantifier phrase takes whom.

studyTips: For each fronted preposition, reconstruct the simpler sentence first: I wrote to her becomes to whom I wrote.
Underline the antecedent before choosing a quantifier phrase: people take of whom; objects take of which.
When a clause ends with comma + which, ask whether which means “this fact”; if so, it comments on the whole previous idea.

exercises.prompt: Ms Shah, to ___ we sent the forms, will reply today.
exercises.feedback: To whom is a formal preposition-plus-pronoun phrase referring to Ms Shah.

exercises.prompt: We had five questions, three of ___ were answered during the meeting.
exercises.feedback: Three of which selects three questions from the identified set of five.

exercises.prompt: The lights went out, ___ delayed the show.
exercises.feedback: Which comments on the entire event of the lights going out.

exercises.prompt: Four students applied, none of ___ had the required certificate.
exercises.feedback: None of whom refers back to the group of four students.

exercises.prompt: The adviser, ___, has agreed to help. (Fact: I spoke to the adviser yesterday. Use the formal beginning “to whom”.)
exercises.feedback: To whom I spoke yesterday fronts the preposition and keeps the object pronoun for the person.

exercises.prompt: We brought four chairs, ___. (Fact: Two chairs were damaged. Start with “two of which”.)
exercises.feedback: Two of which selects two objects from the four chairs.

exercises.prompt: There were three hosts, ___. (Fact: All three hosts spoke two languages. Start with “all of whom”.)
acceptedAnswers: all of whom spoke two languages
exercises.feedback: All of whom refers to the entire group of people.

exercises.prompt: The event ended early, ___. (Fact: The early ending disappointed the guests. Start with “which”.)
exercises.feedback: Which refers to the whole fact that the event ended early.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence by replacing only the formal relative word: The director, with who we negotiated, has retired.
acceptedAnswers: The director, with whom we negotiated, has retired.
exercises.feedback: The fronted preposition with takes whom for a person in formal English.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence by replacing only the relative word: She bought five jackets, none of whom fitted.
acceptedAnswers: She bought five jackets, none of which fitted.
exercises.feedback: Use none of which for objects such as jackets.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence by replacing only the relative word: The internet failed, what interrupted the interview.
acceptedAnswers: The internet failed, which interrupted the interview.
exercises.feedback: Which refers to the preceding event as a whole.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence by replacing only the relative word: We welcomed four new colleagues, two of which are designers.
acceptedAnswers: We welcomed four new colleagues, two of whom are designers.
exercises.feedback: Two of whom refers to two people from the known group.

speakingExercises.prompt: You sent an update to a journalist, and that journalist replied. Say one complete sentence starting “The journalist, to whom” and ending “replied”. Use formal English.
acceptedAnswers: The journalist, to whom I sent the update, replied.
speakingExercises.feedback: To whom puts the preposition before the relative pronoun in formal style.

speakingExercises.prompt: Express the same facts informally. Begin “The journalist, who” and end “replied”. Put to after “update”.
acceptedAnswers: The journalist, who I sent the update to, replied.
speakingExercises.feedback: Everyday English often places the preposition after the verb phrase.

speakingExercises.prompt: Three proposals were submitted. Exactly one was accepted. Say one sentence beginning “She submitted three proposals, one of which” and ending “was accepted”.
acceptedAnswers: She submitted three proposals, one of which was accepted.
speakingExercises.feedback: One of which selects one proposal from the earlier set.

speakingExercises.prompt: Six speakers were invited, and every speaker accepted. Say one sentence starting “They invited six speakers, all of whom” and ending “accepted”.
acceptedAnswers: They invited six speakers, all of whom accepted.
speakingExercises.feedback: All of whom refers to everyone in the group of speakers.

speakingExercises.prompt: The lift stopped; as a result, the meeting was delayed. Say one sentence beginning “The lift stopped, which” and ending “the meeting”.
acceptedAnswers: The lift stopped, which delayed the meeting.
speakingExercises.feedback: Which represents the whole event of the lift stopping.

speakingExercises.prompt: Five applicants attended, and none of them had experience. Begin “Five applicants attended, none of whom”.
acceptedAnswers: Five applicants attended, none of whom had experience.
speakingExercises.feedback: None of whom refers to the five people mentioned.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct only the relative word and say the sentence: “The flight was delayed, what made us miss dinner.”
acceptedAnswers: The flight was delayed, which made us miss dinner.
speakingExercises.feedback: Which can introduce a comment on the full preceding fact.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences. First: four volunteers arrived, and two had training; begin “Four volunteers arrived, two of whom”. Second: the weather improved and this helped everyone; begin “The weather improved, which”.
acceptedAnswers: Four volunteers arrived, two of whom had training. The weather improved, which helped everyone.
speakingExercises.feedback: Of whom selects people from a group; which refers to the whole improvement.

listeningExercises.audioText: The woman with whom I shared a desk has been promoted to team leader.
choices: The woman who used to share a desk with the speaker.
The speaker’s new team leader from another office.
listeningExercises.feedback: With whom I shared a desk identifies the woman who was promoted.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our team printed ten posters, two of which were damaged during delivery.
listeningExercises.prompt: How many posters were not damaged?
listeningExercises.feedback: Two of the ten posters were damaged, leaving eight undamaged.

listeningExercises.audioText: I met six engineers, all of whom work remotely.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three words immediately after “engineers” in the recording.
listeningExercises.feedback: All of whom identifies every person in the previously mentioned group.

listeningExercises.audioText: The shipment arrived on Monday, which surprised us because it was expected on Thursday.
choices: It arrived three days earlier than expected.
It was sent to the wrong place.
listeningExercises.feedback: Monday is earlier than the expected Thursday delivery.

listeningExercises.audioText: The gallery displayed five sculptures, none of which was for sale.
listeningExercises.feedback: None of which was for sale means no sculpture could be purchased.

listeningExercises.audioText: I asked four neighbours for help, three of whom offered to carry boxes.
listeningExercises.prompt: How many neighbours offered to help carry boxes?
listeningExercises.feedback: Three of whom selects three of the four neighbours.

listeningExercises.audioText: Mina, to whom I sent the revised plan, replied this morning.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four words immediately after “Mina” in the recording.
listeningExercises.feedback: To whom is a formal relative phrase referring to Mina.

listeningExercises.audioText: The train was cancelled, which caused several delays on the route.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four words immediately after “cancelled” in the recording.
listeningExercises.feedback: Which refers to the train cancellation as an event and introduces its consequence.
